- Opaque pigments can cover the color beneath and lighten darker passages;
  how much depends on the load. Transparent ones let what is under them show
  through. Try a glaze over the same
  underlayer on the scratch paper first.

## Dry brush

- `b:stroke(path, {dry=true})`, or a brush with almost no water left, makes
  dry contact: pigment lands on the high points of the tooth and skips the
  valleys. The brush keeps its water. The paper's kind and seed decide
  where the stroke breaks.
- Pressure changes the contact width. Check the mark in a 1:1 crop and in
  `relief`, on the scratch paper first.

## Limits of this engine

- **One dried layer.** Every dried pass folds into a single paper
  reflectance. The engine keeps no separate glaze layers and no record of
  which pigment lies where once it has dried.
- **No blotting** and no salt. Neither call is available.
- **Pigment is not conserved while it flows.** The amount of pigment can
  drift as paint moves with the water; `balance()` reports
  `conserved=false`.
- **No sizing or tilt.** Paper kinds differ in tooth and fiber texture, and
  no call tilts the sheet or changes its sizing.
- **Fast clock.** Stages that take minutes on real paper pass in seconds
  here, so time wet work by `balance()` and scratch trials.

## Finishing

- Let the sheet dry (`balance().dry`) before the last look. The studio viewer
  shows the painting in Gallery light by default; `look` with
  `mode="gallery"` shows the same.

Looking at the whole scene now, the far mud bank's top edge reads fine as a distant shoreline, but the mid-ground mud zone feels mushy and lacks definition. I'm thinking I should add a darker mud band closer to the foreground to create more depth separation.

The pink warm pools look flat and tonally mismatched against the golden glow, so I want to add mud spits at their edges and a transparent golden glaze to shift them toward peach. The yellow shine streaks in the far flats are acceptably distant-looking despite some hard rectangular edges.

Looking at the sky, the cloud bars read fine as a stratus band, and the pink ones on the right work too. The boat alone on the mud bank is believable, though a mooring line to a small post and a shadow reflection would add realism. For the left headland, I'm considering adding darker tree/hedge details along the ridge and a soft reflection of the headland shape in the light-yellow water band beneath it — drawn as its own freeform shape with decreasing extents rather than a mirrored copy.

## Handoff — end of sitting 1 (t≈280s, sheet dry)
Title: "Low Water, Evening Glow". Finished for now.

What's on the sheet: blue sky graded through violet cloud bars to a gold horizon glow; violet headland left, faint far spit right; flats in peach/gold with glow-sheen streaks; two mud banks split by a winding pale-blue channel; posts receding along the left bank, a red dinghy on the right bank with a rope to a stake; cobalt pools in the foreground; reed tufts along the bank edges; four gulls.

Unresolved passages:
- Foreground pools are flat, saturated cobalt (cobalt .4 + buff .3 + rose .12, width 12–16, 2µL); a rose .03/ultramarine .012 glaze over them barely registered. A warmer glaze (rose .06, pyrrol .03, naples .08, burnt sienna .02, width 12, 2.2µL) on the small bottom-left pool turned it a dull, stripy tan. Not fixed. I've left them blue as sky reflections.
- The bank tops are fairly straight and banded, and the horizontal row strokes show as stripes in the far flats (y 400–480).
- The pinkish sheen bars (x≈380–470 y 562, x≈690–790 y 572, x≈940–1050 y 562) read as flat rectangles.
- Headland base is a hard straight line; the faint reflection glaze below it (ultramarine .02 / rose .018 / naples .01, width 12, 3µL) softens it a little.
- Unsigned.

Practical lessons (hypotheses unless noted):
- OBSERVED: brush release is front-loaded. For even coverage, top the brush up to a fixed small load every 10–25 cells (my steady()/topup helpers). Width 80, 6µL per 25 cells at speed 3500 makes a smooth wash; width 34, 5µL per 25 cells for mud.
- OBSERVED: pre-wetting with a drop grid of 5µL r80 (~118×95 spacing) gives soft wet-in-wet sky bands that keep their place. 22µL floods, and the pigment runs to the wet boundary.
- OBSERVED: opaque mixes need heavy loads to show over dark mud. Buff-titanium/naples at 0.1–0.15 disappear; at 0.6–0.8 they show as light. Over pale ground, buff 0.16 + naples 0.06 gives a misty veil.
- OBSERVED: thin dark lines need sepia .25–.35 + ultramarine .2–.25. Sepia .15 at width 2 vanished on the mud.
- FAILED: a big scratch trial chunk (≈50 full-width rows of steady() plus waits) timed out. After that every scratch call returned "File exists (os error 17)", even with new_scratch. For the rest of the sitting I ran trials in hidden corners of the painting. Keep chunks small; if scratch breaks again, don't keep retrying it.
- Clouds: a water-only streak, then broken dabs (ultramarine .055, rose .045, burnt sienna .012, 1.8µL) give bumpy-topped cloud bars with soft bottoms.

I've called the painting **Low Water, Evening Glow**.

It's an estuary at low tide in the evening. The sky grades from blue through violet bars of cloud down to a gold glow on the horizon. A violet headland slopes in from the left and a pale channel winds between two mud banks toward the light. Old posts get smaller as they go back along the left bank. On the right bank a red dinghy is tied by its rope to a stake. Small blue pools in the foreground catch the sky, and four gulls cross the glow.

**Unresolved passages:**
- **Foreground pools:** they're still a flat, too-saturated blue. A light rose glaze barely changed them. A warmer, heavier glaze on the small bottom-left pool turned it a dull, striped tan. I've left them blue as reflections of the sky.
- **Flats and bank tops:** the far flats show horizontal stripes from the row strokes, and the bank tops are fairly straight.
- **Pink sheen bars:** the three in the middle distance read as flat rectangles.
- **Headland base:** the bottom edge is a hard straight line. A faint reflection glaze below it softens it a little.
- **Signature:** the painting isn't signed.

**Practical lessons:**
- **Even washes:** a brush lets out most of its load at the start of a stroke. Topping it up to a small fixed load every 10–25 cells gave even washes.
- **Wet-in-wet:** wetting the sky first with a grid of 5 µL drops let the colour bands blend softly and stay in place. 22 µL drops flooded the sheet and pushed the pigment to the edge of the wet area.
- **Light marks over dark mud:** buff-titanium and Naples yellow only show at heavy loads (0.6–0.8). At 0.1–0.15 they disappear.
- **Thin dark lines:** they need strong sepia and ultramarine (about 0.25 each). Weaker mixes vanished on the mud.
- **Scratch sheet:** one very large trial chunk timed out. After that every scratch call failed with "File exists (os error 17)", even when I started a fresh sheet. I tried the later mixes in hidden corners of the painting instead. Keep chunks small.

The full handoff in `notes/journal.md` has the load and recipe details, and marks which broader rules are only hypotheses.
